summary: Extends GMPLS signaling, specifically RSVP, so alarm information can be communicated along a path. GMPLS could already control alarm reporting but not carry the alarm details. The document gives both a functional description and protocol specifics.

plainLanguage.summary: A network can already be told whether to report problems, but it could not pass the actual problem details along. This adds a way to send those alarm messages along the path.

questions: how to report alarms in gmpls rsvp
how does gmpls communicate alarm information
what is the gmpls inhibit alarm communication bit
subtitle: How GMPLS signaling can carry the full list of current alarms along an LSP, in both directions.

tldr.problem: GMPLS signaling could switch alarm reporting on or off, but had no way to communicate the alarm information itself, and error messages report only one problem at a time with no way to say it was resolved.
tldr.mechanism: A new ALARM_SPEC object, shaped like ERROR_SPEC and carried in Path and Resv messages, holds each alarm, with new TLVs for severity, timestamps, a repeat count and a text string, and a new Admin_Status bit (I) to inhibit it.
tldr.outcome: Every node on an LSP can hold the current, synchronized list of alarms for display and diagnosis. It is optional and updates RFC 3473 without changing its procedures.

today: RFC 4783 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3473 by adding new optional protocol elements, without changing that RFC's procedures.

sections.title: The Gap in GMPLS Alarm Handling
sections.content:
GMPLS signaling can already control whether alarm reporting for a label switched path (LSP) is inhibited, using Administrative Status Information and the Admin_Status object of RFC 3473. It makes no provision for communicating the alarms themselves.

The problems that do get reported use PathErr, ResvErr and Notify messages. Those messages typically signal a problem in signaling state and report one problem at a time, which makes it hard to correlate everything affecting an LSP. There is also no way to say a problem has been resolved and its alarm cleared. In optical transport networks in particular, an operator may want to keep an LSP up and report alarms even when the data plane has failed completely.

The extension lets an operator or software obtain the full list of current alarms for the resources supporting an LSP, keeps that list synchronized with real alarm status, and makes it available at every node the LSP traverses. It is optional, controllable per LSP, and not meant to replace data plane fault propagation or change how alarms are processed elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, you could only tell the network whether to report problems. You could not send the list of problems. Now you can, and every stop along the way can see the whole list.

sections.title: The ALARM_SPEC Object
sections.content:
Alarm details look much like error details, so the new ALARM_SPEC object has the same format as ERROR_SPEC but uses a different class number, 198, to avoid error-processing semantics. C-Types 1 and 2 are reserved. C-Type 3 is the IPv4 IF_ID ALARM_SPEC and C-Type 4 the IPv6 one, each defined the same as the matching IF_ID ERROR_SPEC in RFC 3473.

The semantics differ from errors. Alarms usually reflect data plane changes without control state changes, are always tied to in-place LSPs, and mostly help operators and applications rather than the protocol itself. So alarms ride in Path messages, to carry them downstream, and Resv messages, to carry them upstream, giving every point on the LSP the same view. Several alarms are carried as several ALARM_SPEC objects.
sections.plainLanguage: An alarm note looks like an error note, but it goes on the regular letters going both ways down the line, so everybody sees it.

sections.title: The New TLVs
sections.content:
Five new optional TLVs, which must follow any interface-identifying TLVs, work in IF_ID ALARM_SPEC objects and may also be used in IF_ID ERROR_SPEC objects. Types are 512 to 516.

  • Reference Count (512): a 32-bit count of how many times the reporting node has repeated the alarm. It MUST NOT be zero, and a TLV with zero is ignored.
  • Severity (513): a 4-bit Impact (0 unspecified, 1 non-service affecting, 2 service affecting) and an 8-bit Severity (0 cleared, 1 indeterminate, 2 critical, 3 major, 4 minor, 5 warning).
  • Global Timestamp (514): seconds since 00:00:00 UT on 1 January 1970 by the originating node's clock.
  • Local Timestamp (515): seconds by the originating node's own clock, meaningful in that node's context, such as time since reboot.
  • Error String (516): variable-length US-ASCII text, null padded to a 4-byte boundary, whose contents are implementation dependent. More than one may appear.

All but Error String may appear only once per object.
sections.plainLanguage: Each alarm note can say how bad it is, when it happened, how many times it repeated, and a short description in words.

sections.title: How Nodes Handle Alarms
sections.content:
Nodes that support the extension SHOULD store alarm information from received ALARM_SPEC objects and pass them on unmodified: those from Path messages downstream and those from Resv messages upstream. In Resv messages, merging simply means copying all ALARM_SPEC objects received in corresponding Resv messages.

To advertise its own alarm, a node creates an ALARM_SPEC object for each one and adds it to both the Path and Resv messages for the LSP. It MUST set the Error Node Address, Error Code and Error Values, and SHOULD NOT set the InPlace and NotGuilty flags. It SHOULD include interface-identifying TLVs and also Severity, timestamp and Error String TLVs. The global timestamp SHOULD be used on nodes that keep an absolute time reference, and both timestamps MAY be used together. Which alarms to advertise is a local policy matter.

To clear an alarm, the node removes its locally generated ALARM_SPEC from the outgoing messages. Normal refresh and trigger processing applies, and changes to ALARM_SPEC objects SHOULD be handled as trigger messages. The Error Code is the new value 31, "Alarms", with Error Values taken from the IANAItuProbableCause Textual Convention of the Alarm MIB (RFC 3877).
sections.plainLanguage: Each stop passes along the notes it received, adds its own, and removes its own when the problem is gone.

sections.title: Switching Alarms Off with the I Bit
sections.content:
Alarm communication is controlled through the Admin_Status object. A new I bit (Inhibit Alarm Communication, value 0x00000010) means alarm communication is disabled for the LSP and nodes SHOULD NOT add local alarm information. It is set and cleared using the procedures in Sections 7.2 and 7.3 of RFC 3473.

A node that receives or generates an Admin_Status object with the A or I bit set SHOULD remove its locally generated alarm information from the outgoing Path and Resv messages. When both bits are clear and local alarm information exists, it SHOULD add it. Alarms from other nodes MUST be forwarded unchanged whatever the I and A bits say. I-bit behavior MAY be overridden locally by configuration, and when a Notify message is generated for an LSP with the I bit set, the new TLVs MAY be added to the ERROR_SPEC in it.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a mute switch. When it is on, a stop does not add its own alarms, but it still passes along the ones it got from others.

sections.title: Compatibility and Network Boundaries
sections.content:
Support is optional. Because the ALARM_SPEC class number has the form 11bbbbbb, nodes that do not understand it pass it through unmodified, per RFC 2205 rules. So alarm information can be collected across a network where only some nodes support the extension.

The RFC also notes that the extension is a candidate for filtering at the GMPLS user-network interface and the external network-to-network interface. An ingress or egress core node MAY filter or modify alarms, for confidentiality or to show that the core is recovering, and MAY choose not to request alarm reporting on Path messages sent onward.
sections.plainLanguage: Stops that do not know about alarm notes just hand them along. Border stops may hide or rewrite them to keep their inside business private.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some operators may consider alarm information sensitive, so implementations SHOULD let the user disable generation of ALARM_SPEC objects, or filter or correlate them at domain boundaries. The document introduces no additional security considerations beyond those of RFC 3473.

If those protections were breached, alarm information could be spoofed. The RFC argues this would be at most annoying, with slight control plane degradation, because the details are informational and trigger no protocol action beyond message exchange, and a breach that allowed this would allow far worse damage to other parts of the messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Alarm lists can be private, so you can turn them off or filter them. If a bad actor could fake them, they could fake much worse things too.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA created the ALARM_SPEC class (198) in the 11bbbbbb range of the RSVP parameters registry, with C-Types 1 to 4 as described above. In the GMPLS Interface_ID Types registry it assigned 512 to 516 for the five TLVs. It created an "Administrative Status Information Flags" registry listing Reflect (0x80000000), the new Inhibit Alarm Communication (0x00000010), Testing (0x00000004), Administratively down (0x00000002) and Deletion in progress (0x00000001). It also assigned RSVP Error Code 31, "Alarms".
sections.plainLanguage: The new class number, TLV numbers, bit and error code were all written into the official lists.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on generation, ignored on receipt, forwarded unchanged by transit nodes.

fields.name: Severity
fields.desc: Alarm severity, from Cleared to Warning.
